blocks.text: With these matters thus explained, there are three things that will become clear and evident to an attentive reader. I. The mouse called aljarbuo in Arabic is the same as the mouse of Herodotus, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Pliny, Aelian and Photius, which is remarkable for the length of its hind feet and for its leaping. For the Arabs observe [col. 1016] both features in their aljarbuo. They do not, indeed, add that it walks on two feet, because this is a less frequent occurrence. Photius is mistaken when he denies that these mice ever rest on their forefeet. Theophrastus, as reported in Aelian, does not say this, nor does any other of the ancients. II. It is evident that this very mouse is the same as Jerome's arctomys. For it shares a nature with the mouse and the bear; it lives in caves in the rocks and in holes in the earth; and on each rock and hill it has a sentinel on watch, whose negligence is punished with death. III. Finally, اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo is the same animal as the Hebrews' שפן saphan. For all the marks agree, without exception. This is easy to prove. First, neither has a cloven hoof. 2. Both chew the cud. 3. Both are edible, though unclean. 4. Both are gregarious. 5. Both are feeble. 6. Both have their home in the rock. 7. Aristotle, Theophrastus, Pliny and others write that it is an Egyptian animal; and Jerome, that there is a great abundance of this kind in Eretz Yisrael. That Arabia too teems with it, the writings of the Arabs amply show, and Teixeira, an eyewitness, αὐτόπτης [autoptēs], attests it ^{(12)}.

[II, 428] It remains for us to try to explain the various names of this animal. In Hebrew it seems to be called שפן saphan, with Sin, for ספן saphan, with Samech, as if from covering, because it covers the openings of its hiding place with earth, as we have amply shown. Or for צפן tsaphan, with Tsade, as if from lying hidden, because it lies hidden there under the earth and withdraws itself from the sight of men ^{(13)}. In Arabic the same animal is called اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, as if "the fourfold one", because it digs its home في مهب الرياح الاربع [fī mahabb al-riyāḥ al-arbaʿ] toward the blowing of the four winds, as we have learned from the Arabs. And in Chaldee it is called טפזא taphza, from leaping. For that the mouse is ἁλτικὸν [haltikon], a leaper, we are taught among the ancients by Theophrastus, Aelian and Photius, and among the more recent writers by Alcamus, Teixeira and Olearius. The Syriac ܚܓܣ chagas, I suspect, was formed from the Greek χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios], written in abbreviated form thus: χγς [chgs]. Or ܚܓܣ chagas means a lame animal. For among the Syrians a lame person is called both ܚܓܝܣܐ chagisa and ܚܓܝܪܐ chagira. And this little animal seems to limp because of the inequality of its feet. That same mouse was called χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios] from the fatness of a pig, or from its appearance. For the last part of the compound word also means pig. Hesychius: Γρύλλιος· χοῖρος [Gryllios; choiros]. Likewise: Γρυλλίων· ὁ χοῖρος [Grylliōn; ho choiros]. Similarly ὕραξ [hyrax], which is sus [pig] among the Aeolians, is used by Nicander for mouse, because mice παρεοίκασι χοίροις τῶ ῥάμφει [pareoikasi choirois tō rhamphei], resemble pigs in their snout, as the scholiast says there. And from the Greek ὕραξ [hyrax] comes sorex [shrew]. Why the χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios] of the Elders was called ἀρκτομῦς [arktomys] in Jerome's time has already been amply explained. Nor was it without reason taken for the hedgehog, if Pliny writes truly that this kind of mouse has the bristles of a hedgehog: The Egyptian mice, he says, have hard hair like hedgehogs; they also walk on two feet, like the Alpine ones. But he seems to have taken two species of mice indiscriminately. For others distinguish between mice that are δίποδας [dipodas], two-footed, and those that are ἐχῖνας [echinas] or ἐχινώδεις [echinōdeis]. Herodotus: Οἱ μὲν δίποδες καλέονται, οἱ δὲ ζεγέριες, οἱ δὲ ἐχῖνες [Hoi men dipodes kaleontai, hoi de zegeries, hoi de echines]· Some are called two-footed, others zegeries, and others echines, namely from the roughness of their hair, like that of a hedgehog. Aristotle: Οἱ δὲ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μῦες σκληρὰν ἔχουσι τὴν τρίχα, ὥσπερ οἱ χερσαῖοι ἐχῖνοι. εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ ἕτεροι, οἳ βαδίζουσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς δυσὶ ποσί. [Hoi de en Aigyptō myes sklēran echousi tēn tricha, hōsper hoi chersaioi echinoi. eisi de kai heteroi, hoi badizousin epi tois dysi posi.] The Egyptian mice have hard hair, like land hedgehogs. But there are also others there that walk on two feet. I would suppose, however, that the interpreters of Scripture fell into the same error as Pliny and confused [II, 429] these two kinds of mice, and called the mice that are ἐχῖνας [echinas] or ἐχινώδεις [echinōdeis] hedgehogs.
